title: The Bishop’s Hunt
transcript: Black's brilliant idea is to take the white queen, and now, having the only queen left on the board, Black is the only one playing for a win. Or at least you would think so, but this position comes from a chess.com daily puzzle, so we know that there has to be some kind of crazy solution. And indeed, if we start looking for checks, we can find the brilliant bishop to D5. A beautiful little sacrifice that cannot be accepted. Of course, if the king takes the bishop, now there's going to be a knight fork winning the queen. And if the king tries to run this way, there is still going to be a knight fork. So, the king has only one option left to go to B5. Here the king seems to be safe, but White doesn't stop and plays bishop to C4 check. A second brilliant bishop sacrifice. This time, if the bishop is taken, there is going to be a discovered check with the rook, and we're still going to pick up the queen. But most importantly, if the king tries to run back, what other checks do we have? Well, there is rook to A6 check, and because the bishop is preventing the escape of the king, the king will be forced back up, and we will still be able to win the queen. But this shouldn't matter. From this position, the king can run to A4, and now, after something like bishop to B3 check, the king can simply come back up, and it doesn't seem like we have anything better but to just repeat moves and draw the game. So, after bishop to B3 and king to B5, is Black simply out of the woods? Well, not exactly. White has one last incredible move in this position that is going to allow him to win the game. The beautiful bishop [music] to A4. The third sacrifice of this bishop, and this time, the sacrifice has to be accepted because if you move the king away, you're just going to lose [music] your queen. So, Black takes the bishop, and for a brief moment, he is up even more material. But look at this x-ray from the white rook. The bishop is pinned to the king. And so, knight to C3 is actually a checkmate.
